children.title: AI Agents Overview
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/AI Agents Overview
children.summary: This page is the title slide for a presentation titled 'AI Agents Overview' by Yiying Zhang. It indicates that some of the slides were adopted from the website https://llm-course.github.io/.

children.title: What is AI Agent?
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/What is AI Agent?
children.summary: This slide defines an AI Agent by contrasting it with other concepts. It describes an agent as an autonomous entity that operates independently, consisting of a program involving model and tool calls. The content distinguishes agents from LLMs (which lack perception and action) and AI workflows (which are not autonomous or capable of morphing).

children.title: What is LLM Agents
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/What is LLM Agents
children.summary: This page, titled 'What is LLM Agents', illustrates a scenario of an envisioned society composed of AI agents. The central figure depicts various social activities such as cooking in a kitchen, performing in a band at a concert, and making lanterns outdoors. The accompanying text explains how different agents collaborate to perform tasks like ordering dishes, planning, solving problems, and managing finances within this simulated environment.

children.title: Category
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Category
children.summary: This page outlines the categories of use cases for LLM agents, which are powered by large language models. It lists three main scenarios: single-agent applications, multi-agent systems, and human-agent cooperation. A figure at the bottom visually illustrates these three categories using icons to represent a Single Agent, Agent-Agent interaction, and Agent-Human interaction.

children.title: Single-agent applications
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Category/Single-agent applications
children.summary: This page illustrates single-agent applications, featuring a diagram of a 'Single Agent' and a flowchart titled 'LangChain Agent - Sequence Of Events'. The sequence depicts the agent's workflow: Action leads to Observation, which informs Thought, ultimately resulting in a Final Answer. The text explains that LLM agents serve as personal assistants to help users with daily tasks and repetitive labor by analyzing, planning, and solving problems independently.

children.title: Multi-agent systems
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Category/Multi-agent systems
children.summary: The page illustrates the concept of multi-agent systems, featuring a diagram that depicts an 'LLM Master Agent' delegating tasks to specialized sub-agents (Customer Service, Sales, Help Desk) which then utilize specific skills or APIs. The text explains that LLM agents can interact collaboratively or competitively to achieve advancement through teamwork or adversarial interactions.

children.title: Human-Agent cooperation
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Category/Human-Agent cooperation
children.summary: The page illustrates the concept of Human-Agent cooperation, explaining that LLM agents can interact with humans to perform tasks efficiently and safely. It features a diagram titled 'MetaGPT Agents Collaboration with Developing SOP' which details a workflow involving roles like Product Manager, Architect, Project Manager, Engineer, and QA Engineer. The diagram also includes an example of human interaction where a user requests a Flappy Bird game and receives feedback from the system.

children.title: Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol
children.summary: The section titled 'Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol' describes a standardized communication framework designed to enable agents using different frameworks to interact. It outlines the process where a local client agent discovers remote agents by fetching their 'Agent Card', delegates tasks to them, and supports streaming or asynchronous push notifications for long-running tasks. The accompanying diagram illustrates the interaction flow between an A2A Client and an A2A Server, covering discovery, task delegation via messages, progress notifications, and result retrieval.

children.title: Planning:
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol/Planning:
children.summary: This page explains the concept of LLM Agents, specifically focusing on the 'Planning' aspect. It details two key components: subgoal and decomposition, which involves breaking down large tasks into smaller manageable parts, and reflection and refinement, where the agent learns from past actions to improve future results. A diagram illustrates the architecture of an Agent interacting with Memory, Tools, Action, and Planning modules.

children.title: Task Decomposition: Chain of thought
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol/Planning:/Task Decomposition: Chain of thought
children.summary: This page introduces Chain of Thought (CoT) as a prompting technique that enhances model performance by instructing the model to 'think step by step' and decompose complex tasks into smaller steps. It visually contrasts Standard Prompting with Chain-of-Thought Prompting using math word problems, demonstrating how CoT leads to correct reasoning and answers compared to incorrect outputs from standard methods. Additionally, Figure 2 presents a bar chart showing that PaLM 540B achieves state-of-the-art performance on the GSM8K benchmark when using chain-of-thought prompting.

children.title: Task Decomposition: Tree of Thoughts
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol/Planning:/Task Decomposition: Tree of Thoughts
children.summary: This page introduces the 'Tree of Thoughts' (ToT) method, a task decomposition technique that extends Chain of Thought (CoT) by exploring multiple reasoning possibilities at each step. It describes how ToT creates a tree structure through multiple thought steps and utilizes search processes like BFS or DFS, evaluating states via classifiers or majority vote. The page includes a figure comparing four prompting strategies: Input-Output Prompting (IO), Chain of Thought Prompting (CoT), Self Consistency with CoT (CoT-SC), and Tree of Thoughts (ToT).

children.title: Self-Reflection: ReACT
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol/Planning:/Self-Reflection: ReACT
children.summary: The page describes the ReACT framework, which integrates reasoning and acting within Large Language Models (LLMs) by combining task-specific discrete actions with natural language generation. It explains that this approach allows LLMs to interact with environments (e.g., via Wikipedia search APIs) while generating reasoning traces. The text also presents a prompt template structure consisting of repeating 'Thought', 'Action', and 'Observation' steps. The page presents a comparative analysis of different reasoning strategies for an AI agent, titled 'Self-Reflection: ReACT'. It contrasts four approaches—Standard, Chain-of-Thought (CoT), Act-Only, and the proposed ReAct (Reason + Act)—using a specific question about the Apple Remote. The diagram illustrates how the ReAct method successfully navigates search queries to find the correct answer ('keyboard function keys'), while other methods fail or provide incorrect answers.

children.title: Memory:
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol/Memory:
children.summary: This page defines the concept of 'LLM Agents' with a specific focus on their memory systems. It distinguishes between short-term memory, which relies on in-context learning, and long-term memory, which allows for infinite information retention using external vector stores. A diagram illustrates the architecture of an agent, showing how it interacts with tools, planning, action, and both types of memory.

children.title: LLM Agent Memory: Types of Memory in LLMs
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol/Memory:/LLM Agent Memory: Types of Memory in LLMs
children.summary: The page outlines the types of memory in LLMs, starting with a hierarchical diagram that categorizes memory into Sensory, Short-term (Working), and Long-term memory, further breaking down Long-term memory into Explicit/Declarative and Implicit/Procedural types. Below the diagram, three numbered points define these concepts in the context of AI: Sensory Memory involves learning embeddings for raw inputs like text or images; Short-Term Memory (STM) refers to in-context learning limited by the Transformer's context window; and Long-Term Memory (LTM) describes an external vector store accessible via retrieval.

children.title: Agent Memory Types
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol/Memory:/Agent Memory Types
children.summary: The page outlines four types of agent memory: Semantic (facts and general knowledge), Episodic (past requests/actions), Procedural (skills defined in programs or fine-tuned), and Short-term (context within a request execution). The right side features a diagram titled 'AI Agents Memory' illustrating the architecture, including components like LLM, Orchestrator, Vector Database, and various memory types such as Episodic, Semantic, and Procedural Memory.

children.title: Limitations of LLM without external data (Why RAG)
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol/Memory:/Limitations of LLM without external data (Why RAG)
children.summary: The page outlines the limitations of Large Language Models (LLMs) when used without external data, serving as a justification for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). It lists four key issues: static knowledge frozen at training time, lack of proprietary information due to reliance on public data, difficulty in attributing sources of generation, and susceptibility to hallucinations regarding out-of-training-set topics.

children.title: Retrieve-Augmented Generation (RAG)
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol/Memory:/Retrieve-Augmented Generation (RAG)
children.summary: The section titled 'Retrieve-Augmented Generation (RAG)' outlines the core components and workflow of RAG systems. It describes three main stages: Data source, where raw data is chunked and embedded into a vector database; Retrieve, where queries are converted to embeddings to find similar chunks; and Augment and generate, where retrieved context is combined with existing context and fed to downstream LLMs or agents. The accompanying diagram visualizes this process, showing data flowing through chunking and an embedding model into a vector store, which then provides relevant context to a prompt for an LLM to generate a response.

children.title: Why retrieval-based LMs?
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol/Memory:/Retrieve-Augmented Generation (RAG)/Why retrieval-based LMs?
children.summary: The section titled 'Why retrieval-based LMs?' explains that Large Language Models (LLMs) are large and expensive to train and run. It contrasts a standard LM with a retrieval-based approach where an LM interacts with a datastore, suggesting this method can reduce costs and model size.

children.title: Long-term goal: can we possibly reduce the training and inference costs, and scale down the size of LLMs?
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol/Memory:/Retrieve-Augmented Generation (RAG)/Long-term goal: can we possibly reduce the training and inference costs, and scale down the size of LLMs?
children.summary: The section discusses the motivation for retrieval-based language models (LMs) by highlighting that large language models (LLMs) are expensive to train and run. It poses a long-term goal of reducing training and inference costs while scaling down model size. As an example, it cites RETRO (Borgeaud et al., 2021), which achieves comparable performance to GPT-3 on the Pile dataset using 25 times fewer parameters.

children.title: Tool use:
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol/Tool use:
children.summary: The section titled 'Equipping Agents: The Power of Tooling' defines tools as external functions, APIs, or utility agents (such as an MCP server) that LLM agents can call. It highlights that agents have the autonomy to decide when and which tools to invoke. The text lists common tool categories including web search and crawling, browsers, social media and email hooks, and code plus CLI execution.

children.title: Why LLM Agents stand out?
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Why LLM Agents stand out?
children.summary: The page explains why LLM Agents stand out by highlighting four key capabilities: Language Mastery, Decision-making, Flexibility, and Collaborative Interactions. A visual diagram on the right uses a SpongeBob meme format to illustrate the evolution from a basic LLM to an Agent, which combines LLMs with Planning, Memory, and Tools.

children.title: LLMs + APIs to expert models: HuggingGPT
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Why LLM Agents stand out?/LLMs + APIs to expert models: HuggingGPT
children.summary: The section describes the HuggingGPT system, which integrates Large Language Models (LLMs) with expert models via APIs to solve complex AI tasks. The system operates through four distinct stages: Task Planning, where the LLM breaks down user requests into solvable sub-tasks; Model Selection, where the LLM chooses appropriate expert models from a list for each task; Task Execution, where the selected expert models perform the specific tasks and log results; and Response Generation, where the LLM synthesizes the execution results to provide a summarized response to the user.

children.title: LLMs + training for tool use: TALM
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Why LLM Agents stand out?/LLMs + training for tool use: TALM
children.summary: The page presents a diagram comparing a standard Language Model with a Tool Augmented Language Model (TALM). The top section illustrates the basic input-to-output flow of a standard model, while the bottom section details the TALM process, which involves taking an input, calling an external tool to generate a result, and appending that result before producing the final output. The slide is titled 'LLMs + training for tool use: TALM'.

children.title: LLMs + training for tool use: Toolformer
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Why LLM Agents stand out?/LLMs + training for tool use: Toolformer
children.summary: This slide illustrates the concept of 'Toolformer', a method for training Large Language Models (LLMs) to use external tools. It displays four examples where an LLM invokes specific tools—such as a calculator, a question-answering system, a machine translation tool, and a search engine—to retrieve information or perform calculations within its text generation process. The right side of the slide features icons representing these tools: a calculator, a Q&A icon, Google Translate, and Wikipedia.

children.title: MCP (Model Context Protocol)
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/MCP (Model Context Protocol)
children.summary: This page introduces the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard designed to simplify connecting multiple Large Language Models (LLMs) to various external tools and resources. It explains that while direct connections used to be an NxM problem, MCP standardizes this into an N->1->M process using a client-server model where clients request data and servers expose it. A diagram illustrates this architecture by contrasting the complex web of connections 'without MCP' against the streamlined hub-and-spoke topology 'with MCP'.

children.title: AI Agent/Workflow Frameworks
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/AI Agent∕Workflow Frameworks
children.summary: This page discusses AI Agent/Workflow Frameworks, describing them as tools designed to standardize workflows and provide design patterns. It lists examples such as LangChain, LlamaIndex, CrewAI, and Camel, noting their specific strengths like RAG support or multi-agent capabilities. The text concludes with a personal perspective suggesting that for many tasks, using no framework (pure Python) is often the easiest and most sufficient approach.

children.title: What is AI Agent Infra?
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/What is AI Agent Infra?
children.summary: This page defines the components of AI Agent Infrastructure (AI Agent Infra). It outlines four main areas: agent testing and evaluation (including unit tests, benchmarks, and human-in-the-loop), agent autotuning and optimization (covering prompt tuning, model selection, and workflow optimization), agent hosting considerations (serverless vs. long-running, stateful vs. stateless), and tooling, memory, and data.

children.title: Demo Time: Eigent Computer-Use Agent performing a Discord summarization task
children.path: AI Agents Overview.pdf/Root/Demo Time: Eigent Computer-Use Agent performing a Discord summarization task
children.summary: The page displays a title slide for a demonstration. It introduces the 'Eigent Computer-Use Agent' and specifies that the demo will show this agent performing a summarization task on Discord.
